title: Google Business Profile for Real Estate Agents: Eligibility, Categories, Reviews and Posts
seoTitle: Google Business Profile for Real Estate Agents: A Guide
seoDescription: Can a real estate agent have a Google Business Profile? Google's eligibility rules for agents, address setup, name, categories, reviews, posts and what matters most.
excerpt: Agents can have their own Google Business Profile, and most of the wins come from getting the basics right: name, category, address setup and real reviews.
imageAlt: Smiling real estate agent shaking hands with a client and handing over house keys in front of a home with a Sold sign
imageIdea: Real photo of an agent with a client outside a home, daylight, no brokerage logos or readable phone numbers on signs, not staged stock.
author: Michael Shad, Founder of The SocialDM
bodyHtml:
Real estate agents can have their own Google Business Profile, because Google treats agents as individual practitioners, as long as you are public facing and can be reached at a verified location during stated hours. Once you qualify, what matters most is a correct name and primary category, the right address setup, and a steady flow of real client reviews.

Most agent profiles I look at fail on the basics, not on advanced tactics. Here is the practical version, with each rule linked to Google's own help pages.

Can a real estate agent have a profile separate from the brokerage?

Yes. Google's guidelines for representing your business name real estate agents as individual practitioners, and an agent in a public facing role can have a dedicated profile. The brokerage office can keep its own profile too.

A few rules come with that. When several practitioners work from one office, the office gets one profile and each agent gets a separate profile named only after the agent. A solo agent who represents a brand uses a shared profile named in the format "Brand: Agent Name." Support staff should not create profiles, and one agent should not run several profiles for different specialties.

Google's eligibility guidelines also exclude lead generation agents and companies, and a location that is only a rented mailing address. A real estate guide on Google's Business Profile community forum, written by volunteer product experts rather than Google staff, adds that informal internal teams that are not publicly established as their own entity are not eligible. If you run a team, ask whether it has its own public brand before creating a team profile.

Should you show your address or hide it?

Show it only if you meet clients there during your stated hours. Google says that if you do not serve customers at your business address, you should hide it and show a service area instead.

Your situationSetup
You meet clients at a brokerage office during posted hoursShow the address
You work from home and meet clients at propertiesHide the address and set a service area
You meet clients at an office and also travel to themShow the address and add a service area
Your only address is a rented mailbox or virtual officeNot eligible

Google allows up to 20 service areas, and its guidelines say a service area generally should not extend more than about two hours of driving from your base. List the cities or ZIP codes you actually work, not the whole state.

What should your business name be?

Your real name as clients and your marketing know it. Google's guidelines say the name should reflect the business's real world name, and that adding unnecessary information, such as service descriptions or location details, is not permitted and can lead to suspension. "Jane Smith, Phoenix Luxury Homes Expert" is the kind of name that gets profiles in trouble.

Which category should a real estate agent choose?

Pick the one primary category that best describes you as a whole, then add only the extras that are true. Google's guidelines say to use the fewest categories needed to describe your core business, and its category help page says you can add up to nine more.

For most solo agents that means the real estate agent category as primary, while a brokerage with a public office would choose the agency category. Search the picker in your own profile, since labels can change. Avoid adding categories for services you only touch occasionally.

How do you get more Google reviews without breaking the rules?

Ask every client after closing, using the review link from your profile, and never offer anything in return. Google lets you create a link or QR code to request reviews, and its prohibited and restricted content policy bars offering money, discounts, free goods or services for reviews, discouraging negative reviews, or asking only happy clients.

Reviews matter for more than looks. Google says local results are based mainly on relevance, distance and prominence, and that more reviews and positive ratings can improve your local ranking. It also says replying to reviews shows you value your customers. A short, specific reply to every review is a good habit. Never share details about a client's sale in a reply.

Are Google posts worth it for agents?

Yes, as a way to keep the profile current, not as a ranking trick. Google's posts help page lists Update, Offer and Event post types, and its local ranking page does not name posts as a factor.

Good agent posts are short and local: a new listing, an open house, a market note for your area, a closing you can share with the client's permission. One practical warning from Google's help pages: a post with a phone number in the text may be rejected if Google cannot verify the number belongs to the business, and Google's content policy suggests adding a Call button instead.

Posting every week is where most agents fall off. LocalLift Signature is our done for you weekly posting service for agents and title reps, and you approve everything before it goes out.

What matters most, in order?

  1. Eligibility and verification done correctly, under your real name.
  2. The right primary category and an honest service area.
  3. A steady habit of asking every client for a review, and replying to each one.
  4. Accurate hours, phone, website link and current photos.
  5. Regular posts that show you are active in your market.

Your profile is one piece of how buyers and sellers find you on Google Maps and in AI answers. Our real estate marketing page explains how we connect it with search and social.

Questions we hear

Can a real estate agent have a Google Business Profile?

Yes. Google lists real estate agents as individual practitioners, who can have their own profile if they are public facing and can be reached at a verified location during stated hours.

Can I use my home address for my Google Business Profile?

You can verify with it, but if you do not meet clients there, Google says to hide the address and show a service area instead. A rented mailbox or virtual office is not eligible.

Can I put "Realtor" or my city in my business name?

Your name should match how you are known in the real world. Google says adding unnecessary information such as service descriptions or locations is not permitted and can lead to suspension.

Can I offer a gift card for Google reviews?

No. Google prohibits offering money, discounts, free goods or services in exchange for reviews, and it also bars asking only happy clients for reviews.

Do Google posts help a real estate agent rank?

Google's page on local ranking names relevance, distance and prominence and does not list posts as a factor. I use posts to keep the profile current and give searchers a reason to call, not as a ranking lever.
